# SK1133 — A framework copy into the written type is a spread

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`xs.ToArray()` or `xs.ToList()`, where the type it returns is the type the position already names, is `[..xs]`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 14.0 |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | IDE0305 |

## Why

`int[] ids = source.ToArray();` names the array type twice — once in the declaration and once in the method. A collection expression takes its type from the position, so the copy says only what it copies. It is the fluent half of what `SK1001` does for `new T[] { … }`, and the shape a model writes because `.ToArray()` is what most of its training data does. The fix writes `[..xs]` with no space after the `..`: the formatter keeps a spread exactly as it is written (SK-DIV-0009), so that is the spelling that stays. Parentheses around the receiver are dropped, because a spread's operand is a whole expression and none was found that needs them.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
int[] ids = source.ToArray();
List<string> names = query.ToList();
```

Write:

```csharp
int[] ids = [..source];
List<string> names = [..query];
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The fix is safe because the compiler emits the very call it replaces — and that holds only from Roslyn 4.14 on, which is why the floor is C# 14 and not the C# 12 the proposal named.** Measured by decompiling and by running both forms: from Roslyn 4.14 (4.14, 5.0 and 5.9 measured) a collection expression holding one spread lowers to `Enumerable.ToArray`, `Enumerable.ToList`, `List<T>.ToArray` or `Span<T>.ToArray` — the method the source called — so a null receiver throws the same exception (`ArgumentNullException` from `Enumerable`, `NullReferenceException` from the list's own method), an empty copy is the same instance (`Array.Empty<T>()`), and a list's capacity is the same. Under Roslyn 4.8, the compiler that shipped C# 12, every null receiver went `ArgumentNullException` → `NullReferenceException` and every empty array, sequence or query went from `Array.Empty<T>()` to a fresh array; under Roslyn 4.11 `[.. (int[])null]` returned an **empty array** where `ToArray` threw. C# 14 is refused by every compiler before 5.0 (4.11 and 4.14 measured), so a file at C# 14 proves which lowering its build gets. ⚠ **The version must be written down.** `latest`, `latestMajor`, `default` and `preview` are resolved by whichever compiler builds the project, and Skala's own resolves them to C# 14 or later: a project pinned to SDK 8 with `latest` reads as C# 14 here and builds as C# 12 under Roslyn 4.8. Such files are declined — which includes every project that sets `<LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>`, Skala's own among them. An SDK-style project without a `LangVersion` gets its target framework's number (14 for `net10.0`) and is covered. ⚠ **Only receivers whose lowering was measured are taken**, because the compiler chooses the method by the receiver's static type: any reference type through `Enumerable` (arrays, `IEnumerable<T>`, `IList<T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, `HashSet<T>`, `string`, `ConcurrentDictionary` and its `Keys`, queries and classes of one's own, counted or not), exactly `List<T>` through its own `ToArray`, and `Span<T>`/`ReadOnlySpan<T>`. Declined, each because its lowering is not the call: a class deriving from `List<T>` (its `ToArray` becomes `Enumerable.ToArray`, so a null receiver's exception changes); a type parameter (enumerated into a fresh `List<T>`); a struct — one of one's own is enumerated into a fresh `List<T>` and copied out, so an empty one's copy is a new array where `Enumerable.ToArray` returned `Array.Empty<T>()`, and `ImmutableArray<T>` is copied through its span. The call's `T` must be the receiver's element type exactly — `strings.ToList<object>()` lowers to a copy loop, not to `ToList`. The lowering on `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1` is the same call for every accepted receiver (decompiled), so no API is missing on either. ⚠ **No natural type, so only a written target.** The position must name the type: a declaration with an explicit type, a field or property initializer, a `return` or `=>` in a member whose return type is written, an assignment to a plain name, or an argument. A lambda body, a conditional branch (rewriting both branches of one `?:`, each fine alone, stops compiling), `foreach`, `?.ToArray()` and a member access on the result are not reached; `var` and a `void` member's `=>` are reached and refused by the rebinding below (CS9176, and `[..xs]` is not a statement). ⚠ The proposal expected generic inference to break, and for `M<T>(T[] a)` it does not: a collection expression takes part in inference through its spread's element type, `M([..xs])` infers the same `T`, and it is reported; `M<T>(T a)` cannot infer and is not. ⚠ **The target type must be the call's return type by symbol identity** — `SK1001`'s one comparison. `IEnumerable<T> e = xs.ToArray();`, `IReadOnlyList<T>` and `object` targets would let the compiler choose another implementation, and `e is T[]` would stop holding. ⚠ **#425: the rewrite is bound where it stands.** A collection expression converts to every collection type at once, so `M(int[])` beside `M(List<int>)` is ambiguous for `[..xs]`, and `M(params int[])` beside `M(params ReadOnlySpan<int>)` moves to the span (Probe: `array` → `span`); `M(object[])` beside `M(int[])` lands on `int[]` both ways and is reported; `FixRebind.BindsTheSurroundingsAlike` requires the rewritten expression and every enclosing one to bind and convert as they did. Also declined: a user-declared `ToArray` or `ToList`, an extension of that name outside `System.Linq.Enumerable`, `ToHashSet`, `ToDictionary`, any argument such as a comparer, the static spelling `Enumerable.ToArray(xs)`, an expression tree (CS9175), and a comment or directive in the deleted text. Parentheses around the receiver are dropped: a spread's operand is parsed as a whole expression, and a cast, `??`, `?:`, an assignment, `as` and a query all read back bare — the fix asks the parser rather than a precedence table, and declines what does not read back. ⚠ **One defect, one finding.** A receiver that is itself a framework `ToList`/`ToArray` is `SK1081`'s copy of a copy; this rule takes the shortened call on the next pass. A `foreach` over a copy is `SK4006`'s and has no target type here. `SK1001` rewrites a `new`, never a call; `new[] { … }.ToArray()` becomes `[..new[] { … }]` here and `SK1072` takes the array apart after that. With every executable fixture's `Probe` unchanged — a null array, a null list, a null sequence, empty copies and a list's capacity among them — the fix is safe.
